case_scope: Remittance dependence and transnational private-insurance burden stress screen

jurisdictional_mobility_gate.note: Remittances are a major household support rail, but the case stays watch because cross-border support can be survival transfer, fee leakage, or care substitution rather than asset formation.

remittance_or_transnational_support_burd.note: Scale alone does not prove wealth formation; the cube must distinguish consumption floor, emergency support, education/health investment, debt service, and asset purchase.

remittance_fee_leakage.note: Corridor-level cost, speed, transparency, de-risking, account access, and exchange-rate spread are direct leakage channels.

portable_social_rights_for_migrants.note: Remittance reliance must be read with portability of migrant social rights; otherwise families finance risks that destination welfare systems exclude.

bank_account_payment_rail_access.note: Financial inclusion and payment rails determine whether remittance support is cheap, safe, contestable, and timely enough to preserve household claims.

proof_debt: corridor-specific transfer costs and exchange-rate spreads
recruitment debt, wage theft, and job-loss shocks
recipient control by gender/age and intra-household bargaining
payment-rail exclusion, de-risking, and complaint remedies

gate_13_jurisdictional_mobility.why: Gate 13 remains watch: remittances are important, but they can also be private survival taxation across borders unless cost, control, and social-right portability are proven.

gate_16_household_market_extraction.why: Payment fees, exchange spreads, account exclusion, and debt repayment can drain transfers before they become asset-forming wealth.

evidence_debt_register.question: corridor-specific transfer costs and exchange-rate spreads
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Use World Bank RPW corridor data, not global averages, to score cost, speed, transparency, and channel choice.

evidence_debt_register.question: recruitment debt, wage theft, and job-loss shocks
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Link remittance sending to recruitment fees, wage theft, injury, visa loss, and unemployment/job-loss protection.

evidence_debt_register.question: recipient control by gender/age and intra-household bargaining
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Measure who controls remittance receipts, whether recipients can save or invest, and whether care obligations absorb the transfer.

evidence_debt_register.question: survival versus asset-forming use
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Separate food, rent, medical debt, school costs, debt service, asset purchase, business investment, and housing construction.

evidence_debt_register.question: public-service substitution and care burden
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Test whether remittances replace missing public floors in health, eldercare, unemployment, pensions, disaster relief, and education.

evidence_debt_register.question: payment-rail exclusion, de-risking, and complaint remedies
evidence_debt_register.next_evidence: Monitor bank/account access, MTO competition, correspondent-bank de-risking, refund/complaint mechanisms, fraud, and ID/document barriers.

policy_pathway: Score remittances as household-support conversion rails: fee leakage, recruitment debt, recipient control, public-service substitution, and portability determine whether the transfer builds wealth.
Refresh this case on the remittance-price release cadence rather than leaving it as a generic migration note.
